newsitem.title: USA: CBO forecasts 1997 growth of 2.3 percent.
newsitem.headline: CBO forecasts 1997 growth of 2.3 percent.

text.p: The Congressional Budget Office expects moderate economic growth and inflation next year in forecasts issued Thursday that will be used to estimate the budget deficit.
The non-partisan economic and budget analysis agency forecast 2.3 percent economic growth and a 2.9 percent rise in inflation as measured by the consumer price index.
Those figures showed a somewhat rosier economic picture than painted by CBO's previous forecast in May for 1.9 percent growth and a 3.1 percent inflation increase next year.

The projections will be used to construct CBO's budget projections that are to be published at the end of January, and could be revised if "compelling" new economic information is received before those budget forecasts are completed, the CBO said.

The CBO's economic assumptions are "one contributing factor that should make us modestly optimistic about prospects for reaching some kind of agreement" on the budget, Robert Reischauer, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and a former head of CBO, said.
The CBO's economic assumptions are the foundation for the agency's estimates of individual and corporate income, federal spending, tax revenues and the government's budget deficit.
Those estimates known as "technical assumptions" will be used by Congress and the White House in negotiating the budget next year.
If the White House economic assumptions are close to but more optimistic than CBO's, "don't be surprised if Congress accepts them," Reischauer said.

The Republican majority in Congress could say they were accepting CBO's estimates in an effort to reduce friction during the often contentious budget process, he said. The Administration's estimates have been "closer to reality" in the last two years, Reischauer added.
The Office of Management and Budget (OMB), the White House bureau that drafts the president's budget, received the CBO's economic assumptions Thursday afternoon.
"They are important, in the sense that the more we know, and the sooner we know it, the more we will understand the difference in the OMB and CBO starting points," an OMB spokesman said.

The CBO's forecasts for interest rates as measured by the three-month Treasury bill and 10-year Treasury note rates suggest lower government spending on debt service payments, Reischauer said, "that's good news."
The CBO economic forecast also suggested revenues would be up slightly, Reischauer added.
